papers.title: Towards a Langlands Program for Collective Intelligence
papers.keyQuestion: Can a common mathematical language, based on graph transformations and variational information dynamics, unify the study of collective intelligence across diverse disciplines and reveal fundamental structural correspondences?
papers.abstract: The study of collective intelligence currently spans multiple disciplines with distinct mathematical tools, from game theory to dynamical systems. This research points towards a unified mathematical framework, inspired by the Langlands Program, to bridge these approaches. We propose that diverse collective intelligence mechanisms—such as markets, networks, and democratic processes—can be expressed as specialized transformations on graph structures. This graph-centric, variational perspective enables compositional modeling of hybrid systems, multi-scale analysis connecting micro-behaviors to macro-patterns, and understanding of system evolution.
papers.approach: The project proposes using graph theory to represent CI systems, where system dynamics are expressed as transformations of graph structures. Variational principles (like free energy minimization) are used to understand the drivers of these transformations. The research aims to identify and formalize conjectured mathematical bridges between concepts like game-theoretic equilibria and dynamical system attractors, or micro-scale interactions and macro-patterns.

papers.title: Democratic Mechanisms Under Pressure: An LLM Simulation Study of Organizational Resilience
papers.keyQuestion: How do different democratic mechanisms (Predictive Direct, Representative, and Liquid Democracy) compare in maintaining collective utility under varying levels of adversarial pressure, and at what thresholds do they experience catastrophic failure?
papers.abstract: Democratic organizations are vulnerable to adversarial capture due to their openness. This research investigates the resilience of three democratic mechanisms—Predictive Direct, Representative, and Liquid Democracy—against such infiltration. Using a novel approach combining agent-based modeling with Large Language Models (LLMs) as cognitive engines, we simulate democratic decision-making in a resource allocation task under varying adversarial pressure. Our findings reveal that all mechanisms are more resilient than game theory predicts, with breakdown occurring at 70-90% adversarial concentration rather than 50-60%.
papers.approach: The study employs an agent-based simulation where LLM-powered agents, with varying cognitive resources and goals (aligned or adversarial), participate in one of three democratic mechanisms to make collective resource allocation decisions. Performance is measured by resource accumulation and resilience thresholds.

papers.title: Mycorrhiza: A Functional Framework for Multi-Agent Collective Intelligence Simulation
papers.keyQuestion: How can a process-centric, functional programming approach, separating mathematical process definition from computational execution, lead to more robust, verifiable, and scalable multi-agent simulations of collective intelligence?
papers.abstract: Traditional multi-agent simulations often become brittle and hard to verify as complexity grows. Mycorrhiza (GraphTransform) is a next-generation simulation platform built on a 'process-centric' paradigm. Inspired by category theory and functional programming, Mycorrhiza treats system dynamics as composable, pure graph transformations. This approach cleanly separates the mathematical definition of processes from their computational execution, enabling rigorous property verification, enhanced scalability via JAX integration, and modular design of complex collective intelligence models.
papers.approach: The framework is built on category theory, functional programming, and JAX acceleration. Key components include: Core (Immutable GraphState, Property system, Transform composition), Transformations (Pure functions for bottom-up and top-down processes), Services (Interfaces for external services like LLMs), and Execution Engine (Manages transformation application, strategy selection, property verification, and instrumentation).

papers.title: Adaptive Governance Frameworks for AI Development and Deployment
papers.keyQuestion: How can we design governance frameworks that adapt dynamically to rapidly evolving AI capabilities while maintaining democratic legitimacy and preventing regulatory capture by powerful actors?
papers.abstract: As AI systems become more powerful and ubiquitous, traditional static governance approaches prove inadequate for managing their societal impacts. This research develops adaptive governance frameworks that can evolve with technological capabilities while preserving democratic oversight and preventing concentration of power. We propose multi-stakeholder coordination mechanisms that balance innovation incentives with safety requirements, drawing from complex adaptive systems theory and institutional design principles.
papers.approach: We combine empirical analysis of existing governance failures with theoretical work on adaptive institutions. The research involves stakeholder interviews, policy analysis, and simulation of governance mechanisms under different scenarios. We develop frameworks for continuous stakeholder engagement, dynamic risk assessment, and adaptive regulatory responses that can scale across different jurisdictions and technological contexts.
